statements.text: I, for one, am not afraid of the advent of AI. In fact, I want to welcome our future overlords. But I will say, I do see a lot of promise. [...] I also do recognize some of the threats, obviously. To that end, my question for you, Dr. Schmidt, first is that, given the state—the size and scope of the equipment that's necessary today, we're limited to what actors do have the ability to use AI, right? So, at least we know who has access to it, who's utilizing it.
statements.context: House hearing titled 'Advances in AI: Are We Ready for a Tech Revolution?', questioning Dr. Schmidt.

statements.text: AI is going to radically change healthcare to the point where it empowers someone who is a mid-level to be more of an expert in diagnosing more accurate, provide better healthcare standards, the best medical professionals we have today.
statements.context: Rep. Eric Burlison speaks during a House subcommittee hearing on reducing healthcare costs.

statements.text: Given that currently, today, there is the ability to identify graphic content, violent content, and then to often block it or require a person to take some action to basically break the glass and go through and see that content, can that not be applied to deepfake images or things that are created with it? That way, the individual would at least know that there is no truth to this image.
statements.context: House hearing on advances in deepfake technology, with a member questioning a witness about commercial detection of AI-generated content.

statements.text: You are saying that there is tech- nology, AI, that can view videos and images and ascertain whether it is a deepfake?
statements.context: House hearing titled "Advances in Deepfake Technology" on November 8, 2023, during a Q&A exchange between Representative Eric Burlison and a witness.

statements.text: I think of the days, you know, when computers first came out, and you had viruses that were occurring, and people did not know what to do, and now you have antivirus software to address it. I think you are going to have—you are certainly going to have some things—some nefarious things happen with AI, but the counterpunch to that is, you know, white-hat AI.
statements.context: Remarks by Representative Eric Burlison during a discussion of White House AI policy.

statements.text: And I will say that, generally speaking, my attitude on innovation and technology should be—is that we should be laissez-faire. We should be hands-off in any approach, especially to such a new and emerging industry.
statements.context: Congressional hearing examining the Biden administration's executive order on AI, with a panel of witnesses.

statements.text: Yes. My other question has to do with the fact that the executive order establishes an HHS AI task force tasked with developing a strategic plan to regulate aspects of AI in the healthcare industry, including research and discovery, drug and device safety, healthcare delivery and financing, and public health. Could this lead to an onslaught of additional regulations?
statements.context: Congressional hearing or markup examining executive branch AI policy, specifically the reach of the HHS AI task force.

statements.text: We are here today to discuss America's AI ``moonshot.'' Artificial intelligence, or AI, is likely to become one of the most consequential technology transformations of the century. America is seeking to redefine the possibilities of this emerging technology around the globe.
statements.context: Opening statement by the chair of a House Subcommittee on Economic Growth, Energy Policy, and Regulatory Affairs hearing on AI infrastructure and power consumption.

statements.text: Finally, any consideration of regulation of the development and use of AI must account for the needs of innovation and competitive markets.
statements.context: Closing remarks of the Chair at the end of a House Subcommittee hearing on the economics of AI, data centers, and power consumption.

statements.text: But to me, I see the potential for how our economy is going to pivot and grow and the tremendous opportunities that we will receive. [...] Why do you think Americans should be more excited about the prospects and the job opportunities that AI might bring than be fearful?
statements.context: Rep. Eric Burlison posing a question to a witness during a congressional hearing on the economics of AI, data centers, and power consumption.

statements.text: The processes for increasing energy infrastructure required for the operation of power-intensive AI uses are greatly in need of reform, particularly as it relates to permitting and regulatory barriers.
statements.context: Opening remarks at a hearing of the House Subcommittee on Oversight and Government Efficiency on AI economics, data centers, and power consumption.

statements.text: Thank you, Madam Chair, for holding this very critical hearing on the Federal Government in the age of artificial intelligence. As we explore the AI's ability to transform this economy and the potential that it has to enhance Federal program efficiency, combat fraud, and deliver better services to the American people, we must address a fundamental challenge to this, and that is our Federal procurement system.
statements.context: Opening statement at a House Oversight subcommittee hearing on federal AI procurement.

statements.text: artificial intelligence has the potential to revolutionize the world, but also the rail industry, as well. From predictive maintenance to infrastructure for optimizing train operations, AI has the capability to not only enhance efficiency, but reliability and safety.
statements.context: House hearing titled 'America Builds: The Role of Innovation and Technology in Rail Modernization'.

statements.text: And that is the way I think we should think about AI. In fact, AI will be a magnifier for productivity for any individual no matter what they do and, thus, you need the individual. You need that individual that is the core. [...] And I think we are at a place now where we just realize, if we are going to stay on top competitively, we have to be the location for these data centers.
statements.context: Rep. Burlison questions witnesses at a House hearing on AI's future, discussing productivity, regulatory competitiveness, and datacenter infrastructure.

statements.text: a lot of this debate is about what the values that we are going to teach this AI, which I find interesting that we cannot even agree on what free speech means as humanity; how can we trust AI to determine or how can we attribute or provide some kind of values to AI?
statements.context: Spoken during a panel discussion titled 'Shaping Tomorrow: The Future of Artificial Intelligence' on September 17, 2025.

statements.text: My questions are, how do we ensure we are sending more people to go to trade schools for these blue-collar jobs and not just allow- ing them to get laid off by AI?
statements.context: House hearing titled "Shaping Tomorrow: The Future of Artificial Intelligence"; Rep. Crane questions a witness about AI-driven workforce displacement.

statements.text: I think that the vulnerability for each one of us is that we are entering into an era where an AI can devour as much information about you as possible and weaponize that against you, and so that is something I think is a concern, and the question is how do we protect people's rights? [...] which is why I think we should be considering as—on a Federal level having a tighter grip or control on the data about individuals, particularly important data, whether it is the electronic medical record. We may need to do something like what we did with Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA) or extend that beyond just your medical privacy.
statements.context: Rep. Eric Burlison speaking at a congressional hearing titled "Shaping Tomorrow: The Future of Artificial Intelligence."

statements.text: Let an ultraintelligent machine be defined as a machine that can far surpass all the intellectual activities of any man, however clever. [...] there would then be unquestionably an intelligence explosion, and the intelligence of man would be left far behind.
statements.context: House subcommittee hearing on the future of artificial intelligence.

statements.text: I hear a lot from my neighbors on Medicare who are worried about unchecked technology and AI impacting their ability to access care. Dr. Obermeyer, I am concerned about the Wasteful and Inappro- priate Service Reduction (WISeR) Model and what that unchecked AI implementation will do to folks’ abilities to access care. [...] Do you believe that AI systems need independent oversight to en- sure patients are not denied medically necessary care?
statements.context: Congressional hearing on healthcare technology costs, with Ms. Randall questioning a witness about AI in Medicare claims processing.
